title: Barn
description: Agricultural building used for storage and as a covered workplace
wiki_lead: A barn is an agricultural building usually on farms and used for various purposes. In North America, a barn refers to structures that house livestock, including cattle and horses, as well as equipment and fodder, and often grain. As a result, the term barn is often qualified e.g. tobacco barn, dairy barn, cow house, sheep barn, potato barn. In the British Isles and in Europe, the term barn is restricted mainly to storage structures for unthreshed cereals and fodder, the terms byre, shippon or shippen being applied to cow shelters, whereas horses are kept in buildings known as stables. In mainland Europe, however, barns were often part of integrated structures known as byre-dwellings (or housebarns in US literature). In addition, barns may be used for equipment storage, as a covered workplace, and for activities such as threshing.
wiki_excerpt:
A barn is an agricultural building usually on farms and used for various purposes. In North America, a barn refers to structures that house livestock, including cattle and horses, as well as equipment and fodder, and often grain. As a result, the term barn is often qualified e.g. tobacco barn, dairy barn, cow house, sheep barn, potato barn. In the British Isles and in Europe, the term barn is restricted mainly to storage structures for unthreshed cereals and fodder, the terms byre, shippon or shippen being applied to cow shelters, whereas horses are kept in buildings known as stables. In mainland Europe, however, barns were often part of integrated structures known as byre-dwellings (or housebarns in US literature). In addition, barns may be used for equipment storage, as a covered workplace, and for activities such as threshing.


Etymology
The word barn comes from the Old English bere, for barley (or grain in general), and aern, for a storage place—thus, a storehouse for barley. The word bere-ern, also spelled bern and bearn, is attested to at least sixty times in homilies and other Old English prose. The related words bere-tun and bere-flor both meant threshing floor. Bere-tun also meant granary; the literal translation of bere-tun is "grain enclosure". While the only literary attestation of bere-hus (also granary) comes from the Dialogi of Gregory the Great, there are four known mentions of bere-tun and two of bere-flor. A Thesaurus of Old English lists bere-ærn and melu-hudern ("meal-store house") as synonyms for barn.


History
The modern barn largely developed from the three aisled medieval barn, commonly known as tithe barn or monastic barn. This, in turn, originated in a 12th-century building tradition, also applied in halls and ecclesiastical buildings. In the 15th century several thousands of these huge barns were to be found in Western Europe. In the course of time, its construction method was adopted by normal farms, and it gradually spread to simpler buildings and other rural areas. As a rule, the aisled barn had large entrance doors and a passage corridor for loaded wagons. The storage floors between the central posts or in the aisles were known as bays or mows (from Middle French moye).
The main types were large barns with sideway passages, compact barns with a central entrance and smaller barns with a transverse passage. The latter also spread to Eastern Europe. Whenever stone walls were applied, the aisled timber frame often gave way to single-naved buildings. A special type were byre-dwellings, which included living quarters, byres and stables, such as the Frisian farmhouse or Gulf house and the Black Forest house. Not all, however, evolved from the medieval barn. Other types descended from the prehistoric longhouse or other building traditions. One of the latter was the Low German (hall) house, in which the harvest was stored in the attic. In many cases, the New World colonial barn evolved from the Low German house, which was transformed to a real barn by first generation colonists from the Netherlands and Germany.


Construction

In the Yorkshire Dales, England, barns, known locally as cowhouses were built from double stone walls with truffs or throughstones acting as wall ties.
In the U.S., older barns were built from timbers hewn from trees on the farm and built as a log crib barn or timber frame, although stone barns were sometimes built in areas where stone was a cheaper building material. In the mid to late 19th century in the U.S. barn framing methods began to shift away from traditional timber framing to "truss framed" or "plank framed" buildings. Truss or plank framed barns reduced the number of timbers instead using dimensional lumber for the rafters, joists, and sometimes the trusses. The joints began to become bolted or nailed instead of being mortised and tenoned. grok_lead: A barn is an agricultural building primarily used for sheltering livestock, storing crops such as grain and hay, and housing farm equipment and tools, serving as a central structure in farming operations worldwide. Barns originated in Europe and have evolved worldwide, with significant adaptations following early European settlement in North America, where early barns provided multifunctional spaces for animal care, feed storage, and threshing on small family farms. By the mid-19th century, regional agricultural shifts, such as the rise of dairying in New England due to competition from Midwestern grain production, led to specialized designs that consolidated operations and improved efficiency. Barn designs vary by region, cultural influences, and farming practices, reflecting adaptations to local climates, crops, and livestock needs, including medieval tithe barns in Europe for grain storage and rice barns in Asia. In Pennsylvania, for instance, the iconic Pennsylvania barn features a banked construction with a lower level for livestock and an upper level for grain storage and threshing, influenced by Pennsylvania Dutch settlers and suited to diversified farming. English barns, common in northern areas, are typically one-story with three bays for hay storage, animal stabling, and threshing, supporting smaller-scale operations. In Vermont and broader New England, Yankee barns emerged in the early 19th century with gable-end entrances and basement levels to house up to ten cows, while later 20th-century ground stable barns incorporated concrete floors and separate milk houses to meet sanitation regulations for dairy production. Round barns, popularized in the 1890s by agricultural colleges, used circular layouts with central silos for efficient gravity-fed feeding and waste management in dairy operations. Throughout history, barns have adapted to technological advancements, such as the addition of silos in the late 19th century for silage preservation and the integration of electricity and tractors in the 20th century to reduce manual labor. Despite declines in farm numbers due to industrialization, these buildings remain vital to modern agriculture, with contemporary designs like freestall barns providing open housing for dairy cows to enhance animal welfare and productivity. Preservation efforts highlight their cultural and historical significance, linking communities to agrarian heritage and sustainable practices.
